2120:
Breadth means width — the measurement of how far something extends from one side to the other. If you measure a swimming pool and find it stretches 10 meters from the left wall to the right wall, that 10 meters is its breadth.

However — and this is crucial — the word is far more commonly used in a figurative sense to describe the wide scope, range, or variety of something non-physical, like knowledge, experience, or topics. This figurative use is where the word truly lives in modern language.

In its literal sense, breadth simply means width. It answers the question: how wide is this?

"The breadth of the river made it impossible to cross on foot." Here, breadth tells you the river is too wide to walk across.

"The workers measured the breadth of the tunnel before ordering the equipment." They need to know how wide it is.

In this physical sense, breadth and width mean essentially the same thing. The difference is mostly tone — breadth sounds a little more formal and literary, while width is the everyday word. You'd say "the width of this table" in casual conversation, but "the breadth of the valley" in a novel.

Now imagine you are standing at the edge of a vast open field and you look from left to right. The field stretches wide before you. That image — something spreading out widely, covering a lot of ground — is exactly what breadth captures when applied to ideas, knowledge, and subjects.

When used figuratively, breadth describes how much something covers, how many different areas or things it includes, and how wide its reach is.

"The breadth of her knowledge is remarkable — she can discuss medicine, philosophy, architecture, and music with equal confidence." This means she knows about many different subjects. Her knowledge doesn't just go in one direction; it spreads wide.

"The report examined the full breadth of the company's problems." This means the report looked at all the different kinds of problems — not just one or two, but the entire wide range of them.

"He was hired for the breadth of his experience." He has worked in many different fields or roles, and that variety is what makes him valuable.

In each of these cases, breadth is about how many different things are covered or included, not about how deeply any one of them is explored.
Breadth vs. Depth — The Most Important Contrast

The single best way to lock in the figurative meaning of breadth is to understand how it contrasts with depth.

Breadth is about how wide — how many different areas, topics, or kinds of things are covered.
Depth is about how deep — how thoroughly, carefully, or profoundly any one area is explored.

Picture a person who has read fifty books, each on a completely different subject — cooking, astronomy, history, poetry, economics, biology. That person has breadth of reading. They have touched many different fields.

Now picture a person who has spent their entire life reading every single book ever written about astronomy — every journal, every textbook, every research paper. That person has extraordinary depth in astronomy, but their reading might lack breadth in other areas.

This contrast is everywhere in real life:

"The university course gives students breadth across many subjects, but doesn't go into great depth in any single one."

"A good doctor needs both breadth — knowing about many different conditions — and depth — knowing each condition thoroughly."

"His speech impressed the audience with its breadth of ideas, but critics felt it lacked depth."

There is often an undertone of admiration when someone uses the word breadth. When a person says "I was struck by the breadth of her work," they are not neutrally stating that it covered many topics — they are implying that the range was remarkably wide, wide enough to be noteworthy.

This makes breadth slightly different from just saying "many" or "various." It carries a quiet suggestion that the scope is genuinely impressive or substantial.

"The breadth of something" is the most standard construction: the breadth of knowledge, the breadth of experience, the breadth of the problem, the breadth of support. It simply means the full, wide range of that thing.

"The full breadth of something" emphasizes that you are considering all of it, not just a part: "We must understand the full breadth of this crisis before we act." Nothing is being left out.

"Breadth of vision" means the ability to think widely and consider many different possibilities, perspectives, or ideas. A leader with breadth of vision can see the big picture and think beyond narrow or obvious solutions.

"A hair's breadth" is a very common idiom meaning an extremely tiny distance or margin — barely any space at all. "Breadth" here refers to the width of a single strand of hair, which is almost nothing.

"She escaped the falling tree by a hair's breadth." She barely got away — by almost no margin at all.
"The election was decided by a hair's breadth." The winning margin was incredibly small.

This phrase is used whenever you want to express that something was just barely avoided or achieved.

Breadth, as a noun, has two closely connected meanings that share the same underlying idea of wideness. Literally, it is the physical measurement of width — how far something extends from one side to the other. Figuratively — and far more commonly — it describes the wide range, scope, and variety of something non-physical, such as knowledge, experience, or topics covered. The wider the range, the greater the breadth. Its natural opposite is depth, which is about how thoroughly something is explored rather than how much ground it covers. And in the idiom "a hair's breadth," it shrinks to mean the tiniest possible margin.
2121:
A breadwinner is a person who earns money to financially support their family or household. In simpler words, they are the one whose income keeps the family going — paying for food, rent, bills, clothing, education, and everything else the family needs to live.

Think of it this way: if a family were a car, the breadwinner is the engine. Everyone else in the car can ride, but without the engine running, the car doesn't move.

Imagine a household with four people — two parents and two children. One parent goes to work every day and brings home a salary. The other parent stays home and takes care of the children and the house. The children are in school and earn nothing.

In this picture, the working parent is the breadwinner. They are the one person whose earnings feed, shelter, and sustain the entire family.

1. It implies supporting others, not just yourself.
A person who earns money only for themselves is not usually called a breadwinner. The word specifically carries the idea of financial responsibility toward other people — a spouse, children, elderly parents, or other dependents.

2. It can be one person or more than one.

  • Sole breadwinner — one person in the household earns all the income. Everyone else depends entirely on them.
    "After her husband lost his job, she became the sole breadwinner for the family of five."
  • Primary breadwinner — one person earns significantly more than the other, so they carry the heavier financial load, even if the other person also works.
    "He works two jobs and is clearly the primary breadwinner, though his wife also works part-time."
  • Co-breadwinners — two people (usually both partners) contribute roughly equally to the household income.
    "Both of them have full-time jobs; they are co-breadwinners."

3. It applies to any gender.
Historically, the breadwinner was assumed to be the father or husband. Today, the word is gender-neutral. A mother, a daughter supporting her parents, a son, or anyone else who financially carries the household can be called the breadwinner.

4. The pressure that comes with it.
The word quietly carries a sense of weight and responsibility. Calling someone a breadwinner acknowledges not just that they earn money, but that others are depending on them. Losing a job as a breadwinner is more serious than losing a job when you only support yourself, because an entire family feels the impact.

Outside the family context, "breadwinner" is sometimes used in business to describe a product, service, or division that generates the most revenue for a company — the thing that keeps the whole business financially alive.

"The company has many products, but their antivirus software is the real breadwinner."

This is the same idea — one thing that financially sustains everything around it — just applied to business instead of family.
Putting It All Together with Examples

SituationHow "breadwinner" applies
A mother works full-time while her husband raises their kids at homeShe is the sole breadwinner
A husband earns $90,000/year; his wife earns $20,000/yearHe is the primary breadwinner
Both partners earn $60,000/year eachThey are co-breadwinners
A grown son supports his retired parentsHe is the breadwinner of the household
A company's best-selling product funds its entire operationThat product is the company's breadwinner

"Breadwinner" is not a cold, technical word. It carries warmth, sacrifice, and gravity at the same time. When someone is called a breadwinner, it honors the fact that they show up, work hard, and carry others on their shoulders — financially speaking. It is a word that recognizes both the burden and the dignity of that role.
2122:
"Break a leg" is a way of wishing someone good luck — but without actually saying "good luck."

When you tell someone to "break a leg," you are rooting for them to do well. Despite the words sounding violent or negative, the phrase carries a warm, encouraging, and positive meaning.

This idiom is most commonly used just before someone is about to perform or do something high-pressure, such as:

  • Going on stage for a play, concert, or dance performance
  • Giving a big speech or presentation
  • Appearing on TV or in a film
  • Taking an important exam or interview

Examples:

  • Your friend is about to perform in a school play. You say, "Break a leg tonight!" — meaning: I hope you do amazingly well.
  • A colleague is heading into a job interview. You say, "Break a leg in there!" — meaning: Good luck, I'm cheering for you.
  • An actor is about to go on stage. Their director tells them, "Break a leg!" — meaning: Go out there and perform brilliantly.
Why Don't People Just Say "Good Luck"?

This is the most fascinating part of the idiom.

In the world of theatre (stage performances and plays), saying "good luck" is considered bad luck. This is a well-known superstition among actors and performers. They genuinely believe that wishing someone good luck openly will jinx them — meaning the opposite will happen and things will go wrong.

So, to get around this superstition, performers started saying the opposite — "break a leg" — as a way of wishing good luck indirectly. The idea is rooted in old superstitious thinking: if you say something bad, maybe something good will happen instead.

Over time, this expression became so well-established in theatre culture that it spread to everyday language and is now used even outside of performing arts.
Origin — Where Did It Come From?

The true origin of "break a leg" is not 100% certain, but there are several popular and credible theories:

Theory 1 — The Curtain Leg of the Stage
In older theatres, the curtains hanging on the sides of the stage were called "legs." To perform meant going beyond those curtains, past the "legs." So, "breaking a leg" meant actually going out onto the stage — in other words, getting your chance to perform. If you got to perform, you were already successful. This is considered one of the most likely origins.

Theory 2 — Elizabethan Audience Applause
In the time of Shakespeare (the 1500s–1600s), audiences would sometimes stamp their feet on the floor or bang their chairs to show appreciation — rather than clapping. If they stomped hard enough to break the leg of their chair, it meant the performance was outstanding. So wishing someone to "break a leg" meant: I hope you perform so well that the audience breaks their chair legs cheering for you.

Theory 3 — The Understudies Waiting in the Wings
In theatre, an "understudy" is a backup actor who learns another actor's role and steps in if the main actor can't perform. In old theatre, understudies were paid only if the main actor didn't go on. So if the main actor "broke a leg" (got injured and couldn't perform), the understudy got their big chance. Over time, the phrase flipped to become a general good luck wish.

Theory 4 — Bending the Knee (Taking a Bow)
Another theory suggests that "breaking a leg" once referred to bending your leg deeply — as in taking a bow after a great performance. You only bow if the audience loved you. So to "break a leg" meant: I hope you perform so well that you get to bow for applause.

While historians debate which theory is exactly right, most agree the phrase was well established in English theatre by the early 20th century.
Tone and Register — When Is It Appropriate?

"Break a leg" is informal and friendly. It carries warmth and casual encouragement.

You would say it to:

  • A friend, classmate, colleague, or someone you know
  • Someone who is about to perform or attempt something challenging

You would not typically say it in very formal written communication (like a formal letter), though in casual spoken or written conversation, it is perfectly natural.

It is used far more in English-speaking Western cultures (especially British and American). If you use it with someone unfamiliar with the idiom, they may take it literally and feel confused, so it helps to know your audience.
Important: Do Not Take It Literally

If someone says "break a leg" to you before your performance or big moment, they are not wishing you harm. They are cheering for you. Smile, say "thank you," and go do your best.

The correct and natural response to "break a leg" is simply:

  • "Thank you!"
  • "Thanks, I'll need it!"
  • "Thanks so much!"

MeaningGood luck / I hope you do brilliantly
Used whenBefore a performance, speech, exam, or any high-pressure moment
ToneWarm, informal, encouraging
OriginTheatre superstition — saying "good luck" was considered bad luck
Literal meaningIgnore it — it means the opposite of what it sounds like

The beauty of "break a leg" is that it captures something very human — the superstition, the nervousness before a big moment, and the warmth of someone rooting for you — all packed into four small words.
2123:
"Break down" is a phrasal verb — a two-word combination where the verb "break" and the particle "down" join together to create a meaning that is often completely different from the individual words. This is why learners sometimes find phrasal verbs confusing: you cannot always guess the meaning just by looking at the two words separately.

The good news is that "break down" follows clear patterns, and once you learn all its meanings, you will recognize it easily in any context.
The Core Idea Behind "Break Down"

Before diving into the individual meanings, it helps to understand the spirit behind the phrase. Think of it this way:

When something breaks down, a whole thing is either falling apart, stopping to function, or being separated into smaller pieces.

This one idea — a whole thing coming apart — connects almost all the meanings together. Keep this in mind and the meanings will feel natural, not random.
Meaning 1: A Machine or Vehicle Stops Working

This is the most common, everyday meaning. When a machine, vehicle, or system stops functioning, we say it breaks down.

Examples:

  • "My car broke down on the highway. I had to call for help."
  • "The air conditioner broke down in the middle of summer."
  • "The computer system broke down, so no one could work."

How to think about it: The machine was one functioning whole. Now it has "fallen apart" — it no longer works. That is the idea of "breaking down."
Meaning 2: A Person Breaks Down Emotionally

When a person loses emotional control — usually crying or becoming very upset — we say they break down. This often happens in moments of great sadness, shock, stress, or relief.

Examples:

  • "She broke down and cried when she heard the bad news."
  • "He tried to stay strong, but finally broke down at the funeral."
  • "After weeks of pressure, the student broke down in tears."

How to think about it: Emotionally, the person was holding themselves together. Then, under pressure, they could no longer hold it — they "fell apart." Same core idea.

Note: You can also say someone had a breakdown (noun) — meaning they suffered a serious emotional or mental collapse. A nervous breakdown is a common expression for this.
Meaning 3: A Process, Agreement, or Relationship Fails

When talks, negotiations, a marriage, communication, or any process collapses and stops working, we say it breaks down.

Examples:

  • "The peace talks broke down after the two sides could not agree."
  • "Their marriage broke down because of constant arguments."
  • "Communication broke down between the two teams, and the project failed."
  • "The system of trust completely broke down."

How to think about it: What was once a functioning system (a relationship, a negotiation) has now fallen apart. Again — the same core idea.
Meaning 4: To Explain or Analyze Something by Dividing It into Smaller Parts

This is one of the most useful and widely used meanings, especially in academic, professional, and everyday life. When you break something down, you take a large, complex thing and divide it into smaller, simpler parts to make it easier to understand or manage.

Examples:

  • "Let me break down the concept for you step by step."
  • "The teacher broke down the math problem into three simple stages."
  • "Can you break down the total cost? I want to see where the money goes."
  • "Let's break down this essay paragraph by paragraph."

How to think about it: You are taking one big whole and splitting it into smaller pieces. "Breaking it apart" so it is easier to handle.

Note: This meaning is also very commonly used as a noun — a breakdown. For example: "Give me a breakdown of the expenses" means "Give me a detailed analysis showing each part of the expenses."
Meaning 5: To Destroy or Remove a Physical Barrier

When something physical — like a door, a wall, or a fence — is forcefully destroyed or removed, we say it is broken down.

Examples:

  • "The police broke down the door to enter the building."
  • "Workers broke down the old wall to make space for a new room."

How to think about it: The barrier was whole. Now it has been physically "broken apart."
Meaning 6: To Overcome a Non-Physical Barrier (Metaphorical Use)

This meaning extends the idea of destroying a physical barrier into the world of ideas, society, and relationships. When someone breaks down a barrier like prejudice, fear, resistance, or stereotypes, they work to remove it.

Examples:

  • "She worked hard to break down the barriers of racial discrimination."
  • "Good communication helps break down misunderstandings."
  • "His kindness slowly broke down her resistance, and she finally agreed."
  • "Sport has the power to break down cultural differences."

How to think about it: The barrier is not physical, but it is still a "whole thing standing in the way." Breaking it down means removing it, piece by piece.
Meaning 7: A Substance Breaks Down (Chemical or Biological Process)

In science, biology, and chemistry, when a substance breaks down, it is decomposed or separated into simpler components.

Examples:

  • "The body breaks down food into nutrients and energy."
  • "Bacteria break down dead organic matter in the soil."
  • "Over time, plastic breaks down into tiny micro-particles."
  • "The medicine is broken down by the liver."

How to think about it: A complex substance is being separated into its smaller, simpler parts by a natural or chemical process. Same core idea — a whole being divided.
The Noun Form: "A Breakdown"

"Break down" (two words) is the verb. "Breakdown" (one word) is the noun. Here are the most common uses of the noun:

  • A breakdown of a machine: "There was a breakdown of the engine." (It stopped working.)
  • A nervous/mental breakdown: "She suffered a nervous breakdown from overwork." (Emotional collapse.)
  • A breakdown of talks/relations: "There was a complete breakdown in communication." (Failure/collapse.)
  • A breakdown of data or figures: "Here is a breakdown of our monthly expenses." (A detailed analysis divided into parts.)
Grammar: How to Use "Break Down" Correctly

This is important because "break down" is a separable phrasal verb. This means you can put a noun object either before "down" or after "break" — both are correct.

Both of these are correct:

  • "Let me break down the problem." ✅
  • "Let me break the problem down." ✅

However — and this is a key rule — when you use a pronoun (it, them, this), the pronoun MUST go in the middle, between "break" and "down."

  • "Let me break it down." ✅ (Correct)
  • "Let me break down it." ❌ (Incorrect)
  • "They broke them down into groups." ✅ (Correct)
  • "They broke down them into groups." ❌ (Incorrect)

For Meanings 2 and 3 (emotional collapse, failure of a process), "break down" is used as an intransitive phrasal verb — meaning it does not take a direct object. You simply say "she broke down" — you do not break anything; the collapse happens by itself.
Summary of All Meanings at a Glance

1. Machine/vehicle stops working → "My car broke down."
  2. Person loses emotional control → "He broke down and cried."
  3. A process or relationship collapses → "The negotiations broke down."
  4. Explain/analyze by dividing into parts → "Let me break this down for you."
  5. Physically destroy a barrier → "They broke down the door."
  6. Remove a non-physical barrier → "We must break down stereotypes."
  7. A substance decomposes → "The body breaks down sugar."
One Final Tip

The single best way to remember "break down" is to always come back to the core idea: a whole thing coming apart — whether by failing, collapsing, being divided, or being destroyed. Whether it is a car engine, a marriage, a complex concept, a door, a social prejudice, or a molecule — they all share that one common thread. Master that idea, and every meaning of "break down" will feel natural to you.
2124:
To break even means to reach a point where your gains and your losses are exactly equal — so you end up right back where you started, with no profit and no loss.

Think of it like a perfectly balanced weighing scale. One side holds what you spent or lost. The other side holds what you earned or gained. When both sides weigh exactly the same, the scale is balanced. That balanced point? That's breaking even.

You didn't win. You didn't lose. You simply came out even.

Imagine you buy 10 apples for $10, intending to sell them.

  • If you sell all 10 apples for $15, you made a profit of $5. ✅
  • If you sell all 10 apples for $7, you made a loss of $3. ❌
  • If you sell all 10 apples for exactly $10, you made nothing, but lost nothing either. You simply got back the same money you put in. ⚖️

That third scenario is breaking even.
Where Does the Phrase Come From?

The word "even" here is used in its oldest sense — meaning equal, level, or balanced. Think of phrases like "an even score" (a tied score) or "we're even now" (we owe each other nothing).

The word "break" here means to reach or to arrive at a point. So "break even" literally means to reach the point of balance — the moment your gains and losses meet in the middle.

The idiom grew popular in the worlds of business and gambling, where people constantly tracked what they put in versus what they got out. Over time, it spread into everyday English to describe any situation — not just financial ones — where someone comes out neither better nor worse than before.
How It's Used in Real Life

1. In Business

This is the most common and important use. A business "breaks even" when the money it earns from selling things is exactly equal to the money it spent to make and sell those things.

"The startup struggled in its first year, but by December, it finally broke even."

This is actually a big deal in business — it means you've stopped bleeding money and have found your footing.

2. In Gambling and Investing

If you gamble or invest money and end up with the exact same amount you started with, you broke even.

"I spent four hours at the casino and broke even — walked out with exactly the $100 I came in with."

3. In Everyday Situations

The idiom goes beyond money. It can describe any situation — involving time, effort, or energy — where what you put in equals what you got out.

"I spent the whole weekend fixing my car, but the repair bill was as much as the car is worth. I basically broke even."

"She traded her old laptop for a new one, paid the difference, and then sold some accessories. In the end, she broke even."

You'll often hear the related phrase "the break-even point." This is the specific moment or amount at which gains and losses become equal.

"Our break-even point is 500 units — if we sell fewer than that, we lose money; if we sell more, we profit."

Think of it as the finish line you have to cross before you stop losing and start winning.

Breaking even is emotionally neutral in theory, but its feeling depends entirely on context:

  • After a long streak of losses, breaking even feels like a relief and even a small victory. ("We were losing so much money, but we finally broke even!")
  • After expecting a big win, breaking even feels like a disappointment. ("I thought I'd make a killing on that investment, but I only broke even.")

So the same outcome — zero gain, zero loss — can feel either good or bad depending on what you expected.

It helps to know what the phrase does not mean:

  • It does not mean losing a little. Losing even one cent means you didn't break even.
  • It does not mean winning a little. Any gain beyond your costs means you've moved past breaking even into profit.
  • It is not the same as "giving up" or "quitting." It's simply a description of an outcome — a neutral result.

ConceptMeaning

Break even = Your gains and losses are perfectly equal. You spent $X, you got back $X. You put in X effort, you got out X reward. You end exactly where you started — no better, no worse.
A Few More Example Sentences to Cement It

• "After paying for ingredients, packaging, and rent, the bakery needs to sell 200 loaves a month just to break even."
  • "He sold his old car for exactly what he paid for it years ago — he broke even."
  • "The film had a huge budget and barely broke even at the box office — the studio made no profit."
  • "We worked all day cleaning the house before the party, and by the end of the party it was just as messy. We broke even." (Used humorously here — the effort equaled the mess created.)

"Break even" means to reach a point where what you gained is exactly equal to what you lost or spent — resulting in zero profit and zero loss.

If you can picture a perfectly balanced scale — with losses on one side and gains on the other — you'll never forget what this idiom means.
2125:
"Break in" is a phrasal verb — a two-word combination of a verb ("break") and a small word called a particle ("in"). Together, they create a meaning that is completely different from the word "break" alone.

This is important: "break" and "break in" are not the same thing. "Break" alone means to shatter or damage something. "Break in" has its own set of entirely different meanings — and it has several of them depending on the context.

Meaning 1 — To Enter a Place Illegally by Force

This is the most common and well-known meaning. When someone breaks in, they force their way into a building or vehicle without permission — usually by smashing a window, picking a lock, or breaking a door open.

Examples:

  • A thief broke in through the back window while the family was on vacation.
  • The police found evidence that someone had broken in.
  • He didn't have a key, so he was forced to break in.

Key idea: The person entering does NOT have the right or permission to be there. This is why "break in" is strongly associated with crime and robbery.

💡 The noun form is "a break-in" (written with a hyphen):

  • There was a break-in at the jewelry store last night.
  • The police are investigating the break-in.

Meaning 2 — To Interrupt a Conversation or Activity

When you break in, you suddenly enter a conversation, activity, or process that is already happening — without being invited to do so. You cut in. You butt in.

Examples:

  • He was in the middle of explaining the plan when his colleague broke in with a question.
  • She broke in before I could finish my sentence.
  • "Sorry to break in," he said, "but this is urgent."

Key idea: The interruption is abrupt or unexpected. The person doesn't wait for the right moment — they just enter the conversation without warning.

Think of it like someone physically "breaking through" a door to get inside — except here, they are "breaking through" a conversation to get a word in.

Meaning 3 — To Make New Shoes, Clothes, or Equipment Comfortable Through Use

Brand new shoes or boots are often stiff and uncomfortable. When you break them in, you wear them regularly over time until they soften and mold to the shape of your feet. The same idea applies to equipment, instruments, engines, and other things that need a "settling in" period.

Examples:

  • My new hiking boots gave me blisters because I hadn't broken them in yet.
  • You should break in your new leather shoes before the wedding.
  • Musicians often need to break in new guitar strings before a performance.
  • A new car engine should be driven gently for the first few hundred miles to break it in.

Key idea: Something new needs time and use before it reaches its best and most comfortable state.

Meaning 4 — To Train a New Person for a Job or Role

When an organization or person breaks someone in, they teach that new person the skills, rules, habits, and routines they need for a new job or situation. It is the process of introducing them step by step until they are comfortable and competent.

Examples:

  • It took the manager two weeks to break in the new recruits.
  • She is still being broken in — she started only last Monday.
  • The experienced teacher broke in the new assistant by showing her how the classroom worked.

Key idea: A new person is "stiff and unfamiliar" just like a new pair of shoes. Breaking them in means helping them become comfortable and effective in their new environment.

Meaning 5 — To Tame or Train an Animal (Especially a Horse)

This meaning is closely related to Meaning 4, but it is used specifically for animals. When you break in a wild or untrained animal, you train it to accept human control and commands.

Examples:

  • Cowboys in the American West were known for breaking in wild horses.
  • It can take months to fully break in a young horse for riding.

Key idea: A wild animal resists control, just like a stiff shoe resists your foot. "Breaking it in" means overcoming that resistance through training until the animal cooperates.
How to Tell the Meanings Apart

Context is everything. Ask yourself:

  • Is someone entering a place without permission? → Illegal entry (Meaning 1)
  • Is someone interrupting a speech or conversation? → Interruption (Meaning 2)
  • Is it about new objects or equipment becoming comfortable? → Softening through use (Meaning 3)
  • Is it about a new employee or person being taught a role? → Training a new person (Meaning 4)
  • Is it about a wild animal being trained? → Taming an animal (Meaning 5)
Grammar: How "Break In" Works in a Sentence

"Break in" is a separable phrasal verb for Meanings 3, 4, and 5. This means you can place the object between "break" and "in":

  • I need to break in my shoes. ✅
  • I need to break my shoes in. ✅ (Both are correct.)

However, if you use a pronoun (like them, it, him, her), you must separate the phrasal verb:

  • I need to break them in. ✅
  • I need to break in them. ❌ (Wrong!)

For Meanings 1 and 2, "break in" is typically inseparable — nothing goes between the two words:

  • Someone broke in. ✅
  • She broke in with a question. ✅

FormExample
Basebreak in
Presentbreaks in

Past participlebroken in

Here are the forms with examples:

  • Base form: They plan to break in tonight.
  • Present (he/she/it): The thief breaks in from the back.
  • Past simple: Someone broke in last night.
  • Present participle: He is breaking in his new boots.
  • Past participle: The horses have all been broken in.

Knowing synonyms will help you understand the meaning more deeply.

Meaning 1 (illegal entry): burglarize, force entry, trespass, intrude

Meaning 2 (interrupt): butt in, cut in, interject, chime in

Meaning 3 (soften through use): wear in, loosen up, soften

Meaning 4 (train a new person): orient, onboard, train, induct

Meaning 5 (tame an animal): tame, train, domesticate

Mistake 1 — Confusing "break in" with "break into"

These are closely related but slightly different in structure.

  • "Break in" is used without directly naming the place: "A thief broke in."
  • "Break into" is used when you name the specific place: "A thief broke into the shop."

Both are correct — you just choose based on whether you are naming the place or not.

Mistake 2 — Using "break" alone instead of "break in"

Saying "He broke the house" means he destroyed the house. Saying "He broke into the house" means he entered illegally. These are very different!

Mistake 3 — Forgetting the noun form needs a hyphen

The verb is two words: break in. The noun is hyphenated: a break-in. Do not write "a break in" (without hyphen) when you mean the noun, as it changes the meaning to something else entirely — for example, "a break in the clouds" means a gap or pause in the clouds, not a burglary.

"Break in" is one English phrase with five distinct lives:

  1. Enter illegally by force — a thief breaking into a house
  2. Interrupt — cutting into a conversation suddenly
  3. Soften something new through use — wearing in stiff new shoes
  4. Train a new person — introducing someone to a new job
  5. Tame an animal — training a wild horse

The noun form is "a break-in" and refers to an illegal entry. The correct meaning always depends on the context surrounding the phrase, so when you see "break in," look at what is around it to figure out which meaning applies.
2126: "Break off" is a phrasal verb — that means it is a verb ("break") combined with a small word ("off") to create a new, specific meaning. Phrasal verbs are very common in English, and the combined meaning is often different from the individual words. "Break off" has several meanings, and you need to understand all of them to truly master this phrase.
Meaning 1 — To Physically Separate a Piece from Something

This is the most literal meaning. When you "break off" a piece of something, you snap, detach, or remove it from the main object by force. The piece separates — it comes away from the rest.

Examples:

  • She broke off a square of chocolate and handed it to the child.
  • He broke off a branch from the tree to use as a walking stick.
  • The handle broke off when I pulled too hard.
  • A piece of the cliff broke off and fell into the sea.

Key idea: Something that was attached is now detached — usually suddenly, and often with a snapping action.
Meaning 2 — To Suddenly Stop Speaking

When a person "breaks off" while talking, they stop in the middle of what they were saying — abruptly, without finishing the sentence or thought. This usually happens because something surprised them, distracted them, or made them feel emotional.

Examples:

  • She broke off mid-sentence when she saw him walk through the door.
  • He was explaining the plan, then broke off — he seemed too upset to continue.
  • The teacher broke off and stared at the student who had just interrupted.
  • She broke off suddenly, as if she had said too much.

Key idea: The speech stops abruptly — not at a natural ending point, but in the middle, due to emotion, surprise, or distraction.
Meaning 3 — To End a Relationship

When someone "breaks off" a relationship, an engagement, or a friendship, they deliberately end it — they bring it to a stop. This meaning is used especially for romantic relationships and engagements.

Examples:

  • She broke off the engagement just two weeks before the wedding.
  • He broke off their friendship after the argument.
  • They broke things off after dating for three years.
  • She decided to break it off because they wanted different things in life.

Key idea: A personal relationship comes to a deliberate, often permanent end. The person doing it is making a conscious choice.

💡 Note: In everyday speech, people often say "break it off" or "break things off" for this meaning — especially for romantic relationships.
Meaning 4 — To End Formal Talks, Negotiations, or Relations

This meaning is used in formal, professional, or political contexts. When two parties (companies, governments, teams) "break off" discussions or relations, they stop the process entirely — often because of a disagreement or conflict.

Examples:

  • The two countries broke off diplomatic relations after the conflict.
  • The company broke off negotiations when the two sides could not agree on a price.
  • Talks broke off after the union rejected the company's offer.
  • They had to break off discussions and start over from the beginning.

Key idea: A formal process or official relationship between parties is brought to a halt — often suddenly and due to tension.
Meaning 5 — To Stop an Activity (Often to Take a Break)

"Break off" can also simply mean to stop doing something, either temporarily (like pausing for lunch) or permanently. This is a more general use, and it often does not require an object.

Examples:

  • Let's break off here and continue the meeting after lunch.
  • The search team broke off at nightfall and resumed the next morning.
  • They broke off work early on Friday.
  • We broke off the discussion and agreed to think about it overnight.

Key idea: An activity is paused or stopped — the focus is on the act of stopping, not on something being destroyed or ended permanently.
Grammar Notes — How to Use "Break Off" Correctly

This is important for a learner. Here is what you need to know:

It can be transitive (with an object) or intransitive (without an object):

  • Transitive: She broke off the engagement. (There is an object: "the engagement")
  • Intransitive: The branch broke off. (No object — the thing just breaks off by itself)

When you use a pronoun as the object, it must go in the middle:

  • ✅ She broke it off. (Correct)
  • ❌ She broke off it. (Incorrect)

But with a noun, both positions are possible:

  • ✅ She broke off the engagement.
  • ✅ She broke the engagement off.

Tense forms:

FormExample
Basebreak off
Past simplebroke off
Past participlebroken off
Present participlebreaking off
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "break off" has multiple meanings, the context tells you which one applies. Here is a simple guide:

  • If it involves a physical object snapping or detaching → Meaning 1
  • If it involves a person stopping their speech mid-sentence → Meaning 2
  • If it involves a romantic or personal relationship ending → Meaning 3
  • If it involves governments, companies, or formal talks ending → Meaning 4
  • If it involves stopping an activity or taking a pause → Meaning 5
The Common Thread in All Meanings

Even though the meanings seem different, they all share one core idea:

Something that was connected, continuing, or attached comes to a stop or gets separated.

Whether it is a piece of chocolate, a conversation, a romance, a diplomatic relationship, or a work session — in every case, something that was going on or was joined together is now broken away or cut off.
Quick Summary

MeaningSimple DefinitionExample
Physical separationA piece snaps off from the wholeBreak off a piece of bread
Stopping speechSuddenly stop talking mid-sentenceShe broke off when she heard the bang
Ending a relationshipDeliberately end a romantic/personal bondHe broke off the engagement
Ending formal talksStop negotiations or diplomatic tiesThe countries broke off relations
Stopping an activityPause or stop doing somethingLet's break off for the day
A Few Natural Phrases You'll Hear Often

• "Break it off" → End a romantic relationship
  • "Break off a piece" → Detach a portion physically
  • "Break off talks/negotiations" → End formal discussions
  • "Break off mid-sentence" → Stop speaking abruptly
  • "Break off for lunch/the day" → Stop working temporarily

That is everything you need to know about "break off." The phrase is flexible, but once you understand the core idea of separation or stopping, all its meanings will feel natural and logical to you.
2127:
Before learning the individual meanings, understand the soul of this phrase. "Break" suggests something suddenly bursting, splitting, or forcing its way through. "Out" suggests movement from the inside to the outside, or something becoming visible that wasn't before.

Put them together, and "break out" almost always carries the feeling of something sudden, forceful, or unexpected happening — either physically or figuratively. Hold that feeling in your mind. It will help every meaning below make intuitive sense.

1. To Escape by Force

This is the most literal meaning. When a person or animal breaks out, they force their way out of a place that was meant to contain them.

  • Three prisoners broke out of the high-security jail last night.
  • The dog broke out of its kennel and ran down the street.
  • He broke out of the room and ran as fast as he could.

The key here is force and confinement. There is a barrier, and someone actively pushes through it. This is different from simply "leaving," which is calm and permitted. Breaking out is urgent, often against the rules, and involves overcoming something.

2. To Start Suddenly (Especially Something Bad)

This is one of the most common uses. When something like a fire, a war, a riot, or a disease breaks out, it starts suddenly, unexpectedly, and with intensity. No one planned for it to happen at that exact moment.

  • A massive fire broke out in the warehouse early this morning.
  • Fighting broke out between the two groups after the match.
  • War broke out between the two neighbouring countries.
  • A new disease broke out in the southern region.
  • Panic broke out when the lights suddenly went off.

Notice that this meaning is almost always used for things that are negative, dangerous, or uncontrolled — fire, war, violence, disease, panic, protests, riots. You would not say "A party broke out" in standard usage, because a party is positive and planned. The phrase carries a sense of alarm.

3. To Suddenly Appear on Your Skin

When a rash, spots, pimples, or sweat break out, they appear on your skin suddenly and often because of stress, illness, heat, or an allergic reaction. The structure is usually: break out in something.

  • She broke out in a rash after eating strawberries.
  • He broke out in hives when he touched the cat.
  • I always break out in spots when I'm stressed.
  • The runner broke out in a sweat after just five minutes.
  • The cold wind made her break out in goosebumps.

The phrase works beautifully here because the spots or sweat are literally breaking through the surface of the skin — bursting outward. The core idea of "breaking out" maps perfectly onto this physical event.

4. To Suddenly Start Doing Something (With Emotion or Energy)

People can also "break out" into an action, especially one driven by strong emotion. This is always followed by "in" or "into."

  • The entire crowd broke out in cheers when the team scored.
  • She broke out into laughter in the middle of the serious meeting.
  • The children broke out in song when they heard the music.
  • He broke out into a sprint when he saw the bus arriving.
  • The audience broke out into applause at the end of the performance.

Here, the emotion or action was building up quietly on the inside, and then it suddenly burst outward — just like the core idea of the phrase.

5. To Take Something Out for Use (Especially for a Special Occasion)

In casual, everyday speech, "break out" can mean to bring something out and make it available to use — often something that was being saved or stored for the right moment.

  • It's a celebration — let's break out the champagne!
  • He broke out his finest suit for the wedding.
  • The host broke out a beautiful old bottle of wine for her guests.
  • Break out the snacks — the game is about to start!
  • The soldiers broke out the emergency supplies after the storm.

This use has a slightly festive or dramatic feel. You're not just "getting" something — you're producing it with a sense of occasion or urgency.

6. To Become Suddenly Famous or Successful

In the world of entertainment, music, sports, or business, when someone breaks out, they suddenly move from being unknown or underrated to being famous, recognized, or highly successful.

  • She broke out as a singer after her second album went viral.
  • The young actor finally broke out after years of small roles.
  • He broke out onto the international stage with a record-breaking performance.
  • The startup broke out and became one of the fastest-growing companies in the industry.

The imagery here is powerful: the person was confined inside obscurity, and then they forced their way out into public attention. Again, the core idea works perfectly.

7. To Escape From a Difficult Situation or Pattern (Figurative)

You can also "break out of" something that is not a physical place — a habit, a routine, a bad situation, a way of thinking.

  • She desperately wanted to break out of her boring daily routine.
  • He finally broke out of the cycle of debt after years of struggle.
  • Breaking out of your comfort zone is the first step to real growth.
  • She broke out of the pattern of negative thinking that had held her back.

This use is metaphorical. The "prison" here is not made of walls — it's made of circumstances, habits, or mental patterns. But the effort to escape is just as real.

8. To Separate or Categorize Information (Business/Professional Use)

In professional and business contexts, "break out" means to separate a large set of information into specific, smaller categories so it is easier to understand.

  • Could you break out the sales figures by region?
  • The report breaks out the total cost into three separate categories.
  • Let's break out the data by age group so we can see the trends more clearly.
  • Can you break out which expenses are travel-related?

Here, you are taking something whole and pulling parts of it out so each part can be seen clearly on its own.

When you remove the space and write it as one word — breakout — it becomes a noun or an adjective with its own set of meanings.

As a noun:

  • A prison breakout = an escape from prison. The breakout was planned for months.
  • A skin breakout / acne breakout = when pimples or spots appear on your face. I've been getting breakouts lately.
  • A breakout session = at a conference or large meeting, smaller groups go to separate rooms for focused discussions. These smaller sessions are called breakout sessions.

As an adjective:

  • A breakout performance = a performance so impressive that it makes someone famous overnight. Her breakout performance in that film changed her career.
  • A breakout year = a year when someone suddenly becomes very successful. 2023 was his breakout year.
  • A breakout role = the role that first made an actor or actress famous.
  • A breakout star = someone who has recently and suddenly become very famous.
How to Know Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "break out" has so many meanings, context is your best guide. Here's a simple way to think about it:

  • Person + break out + of + enclosed place → Escape (e.g., broke out of prison)
  • Event/disaster + break out → Sudden start of something bad (e.g., fire broke out)
  • Person + break out + in/into + skin condition or emotion → Skin reaction or sudden burst of emotion (e.g., broke out in a rash / broke out in laughter)
  • Person + break out + something → Taking something out for use (e.g., break out the champagne)
  • Person + break out (in entertainment/career context) → Becoming famous
  • Person + break out + of + abstract situation → Escaping a pattern or habit
  • Break out data/figures → Separating into categories
The One Thread That Ties Everything Together

No matter which meaning you encounter, "break out" always involves something moving from a state of being contained, hidden, or held back — to being suddenly released, visible, or active. A prisoner breaks out of a cell. Fire breaks out of control. Spots break out through the skin. Fame breaks out from years of obscurity. Data breaks out from a lump sum into clear categories.

Once you see that single thread running through all the meanings, the phrase will never confuse you again.
2128:
To understand this idiom, you need to picture a military formation. Soldiers stand in neat, organized rows and lines — those lines are called ranks. Every soldier is expected to stand perfectly still, face the same direction, and move as one unified group. If one soldier steps out of that line — moves independently, breaks away from the formation — they have broken ranks.

That image is the seed of the idiom.
What It Means Today

In modern, everyday English, "break ranks" means:

To publicly disagree with, or act against, the group, organization, or authority you belong to — especially when others in that group are staying silent or going along.

It's not just about disagreeing privately in your own head. Breaking ranks means you openly defy or go against the official position of your group, often at personal risk or cost. The key element is the public act of separation — you are visibly stepping away from the group line.
The Core Idea in One Simple Thought
Imagine everyone in your group is expected to say "yes." You say "no" — openly, in front of others. You have broken ranks.
What Makes This Idiom Special

Three ingredients are almost always present:

1. There is a group with a shared position.
This could be a political party, a company, a team, a family, or any organization where members are expected to think or act alike.

2. There is pressure to conform.
The group expects loyalty and unity. Speaking out is not the easy or safe choice.

3. Someone chooses to speak out or act differently anyway.
That person breaks ranks — they prioritize their own conscience, judgment, or honesty over group loyalty.
Real-Life Examples

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how widely it is used:

Politics:
"Three senators broke ranks with their party and voted against the new tax bill."
→ Most senators voted together. Three chose to go against their own party publicly.

Business:
"A senior executive broke ranks and told the media that the company had been hiding its financial losses."
→ The company expected silence. The executive chose honesty over loyalty.

Sports:
"The player broke ranks with his teammates by criticizing the coach in an interview."
→ The rest of the team stayed quiet. He spoke out alone.

Family:
"She broke ranks with her family by supporting her brother's decision to drop out of college, even though everyone else disapproved."
→ The whole family was against it. She was the only one who publicly supported him.

Science or academia:
"The scientist broke ranks with the rest of the research community by questioning the widely accepted theory."
→ Most scientists agreed on the theory. She openly challenged it.
The Tone and Feeling of the Idiom

This is important: the idiom carries a neutral-to-positive feeling in most modern contexts, but it depends entirely on your point of view.

  • If you admire the person who speaks out, you see breaking ranks as brave, honest, and principled.
  • If you value group loyalty, you might see it as disloyal, disruptive, or even a betrayal.

The idiom itself does not judge. It simply describes the act. The speaker's tone tells you how to feel about it.
What "Ranks" Refers To in the Idiom

In modern usage, "ranks" no longer means soldiers in a line. It now broadly refers to membership in a group — especially when that group has a shared position or official stance. When you are in the ranks of a party, company, or team, you are a member who is expected to follow the group line. When you break those ranks, you are stepping out of that membership role by acting against the group.
Grammar: How Is It Used?

It is a verb phrase. The verb "break" changes depending on the sentence:

  • Present: He breaks ranks when he disagrees.
  • Past: She broke ranks yesterday.
  • Present continuous: They are breaking ranks over this issue.
  • Perfect: He has broken ranks before.

It is often followed by "with" to specify which group is being defied:

  • "She broke ranks with the union."
  • "He broke ranks with his own government."

Without "with," the group is usually understood from context.
Similar Idioms and Phrases

Understanding related expressions will strengthen your grasp:

  • "Go against the grain" — to act against what is normal or expected (broader; not necessarily about a group).
  • "Rock the boat" — to cause trouble by challenging the status quo (usually milder; more about causing disruption than a strong public stand).
  • "Blow the whistle" — to expose wrongdoing publicly (more specific; focuses on revealing secrets or misconduct).
  • "Toe the line / toe the party line" — the opposite of breaking ranks; it means to obey and conform to the group's position.
  • "Speak out" — to voice your opinion publicly, often against something (similar spirit, but less group-focused).
A Quick Way to Always Remember It

Picture a soldier stepping out of a perfectly straight military line. Everyone else stays in formation. That one soldier has broken the rank — the line. Now replace "military line" with any group, institution, or organization. The moment someone steps out and goes their own way publicly, they break ranks.

Conformity = staying in the ranks. Public defiance = breaking ranks.
Summary in One Sentence

"Break ranks" means to openly disagree with or act against the official position of a group you belong to, especially when others in that group are staying silent or going along — often requiring courage, and often carrying a personal cost.
2129:
To "break the ice" means to do or say something that helps people feel more comfortable and relaxed, especially in an awkward, tense, or unfamiliar social situation — like when strangers first meet, or when a conversation feels stiff and uneasy.

It is the act of removing that invisible wall of awkwardness between people so that a natural, friendly interaction can begin.

Think of it this way: imagine you walk into a room full of people you don't know. Everyone is standing quietly, feeling a little shy or uncomfortable. Nobody knows what to say. Then one person cracks a funny joke, and suddenly everyone laughs and starts talking. That person just broke the ice.
The Literal Origin — Where This Idiom Comes From

To truly understand any idiom, it helps to understand where it was born. This one has a fascinating, very literal history.

Centuries ago, before modern technology, winter was a serious problem for ships and trade. Rivers and harbours would freeze over with thick layers of ice during cold months. This meant trade ships — carrying food, goods, and supplies — were completely trapped and could not move. This brought commerce to a standstill and caused serious economic hardship.

To solve this, smaller, stronger vessels called "ice-breaker ships" were sent out first. Their job was to physically smash through the frozen ice, carving a path through the water so that the larger trade ships could follow and reach their destination. Once the ice was broken, everything could flow freely again.

This is the origin of the metaphor:

  • The frozen ice = the tension, awkwardness, or barrier between people
  • Breaking the ice = removing that barrier so that communication and warmth can flow freely

Over time, people started using it to describe social situations where someone "smashes through" that invisible wall of awkwardness, just like those ships smashed through frozen water.

The phrase has been around in English for a very long time. It was already being used figuratively by the 17th century, and the poet Samuel Butler used a form of it in his 1663 satirical poem Hudibras, showing just how old and deeply rooted this expression is in the English language.
How to Use It — Grammar & Structure

"Break the ice" is a verb phrase (an idiom built around an action). Here is how it works grammatically:

Common structures:

StructureExample

1. To break the ice
→ "Someone needs to break the ice at this party."

2. Break the ice + by doing something
→ "She broke the ice by telling a funny story."
→ "He broke the ice by offering everyone a cup of coffee."

3. Something breaks the ice
→ "A shared laugh really broke the ice between them."
→ "That game broke the ice for us all."

4. An icebreaker (noun form)
→ When the thing used to break the ice is being described, it is called an *"icebreaker."
→ "The teacher started class with an icebreaker activity."
→ "His joke was a great icebreaker."
When Do People Use This Idiom?

"Break the ice" is used in a very wide range of real-life situations. Here are the most common ones:

1. Meeting new people
When strangers are introduced — at a party, a networking event, a new school, or a new job — the first moments are often awkward. Breaking the ice means doing or saying something to get a natural conversation going.
→ "It was our first day at the new office, so I broke the ice by bringing donuts for everyone."

2. Starting a difficult conversation
Sometimes people need to have a tough, sensitive, or uncomfortable discussion. The person who decides to speak first, despite the tension, is "breaking the ice."
→ "Nobody wanted to talk about the problem, so Maria broke the ice and brought it up directly."

3. A first date
First dates are notoriously awkward. A funny comment, a playful question, or a shared activity can break the ice and make both people feel at ease.
→ "He broke the ice on their first date by asking her the silliest 'would you rather' questions."

4. Business meetings or negotiations
Before serious talks begin, people sometimes use small talk, a joke, or a light activity to loosen the atmosphere and build a sense of trust.
→ "The negotiators broke the ice with a casual lunch before sitting down to discuss the contract."

5. Team settings or classrooms
Teachers, managers, and team leaders often use "icebreaker" games or questions at the start of a new group activity to help everyone feel comfortable with one another.
→ "The coach started training camp with icebreaker exercises so the new players could bond quickly."

Here are clear, natural examples showing the idiom used in different tones and contexts:

Casual / Social:

  • "Nobody was talking at the party until Jake broke the ice with his hilarious impression of the host."
  • "She broke the ice by complimenting his shoes, and they ended up talking for two hours."

Professional:

  • "The CEO broke the ice at the conference by sharing a personal story about his biggest failure."
  • "We used a quick icebreaker game before the meeting so everyone could relax."

Romantic:

  • "He had been nervous to talk to her for weeks, but finally broke the ice by asking if she'd seen the new movie."

Difficult / Serious situations:

  • "The silence between the old friends had lasted two years. It was her letter that finally broke the ice."
  • "Nobody wanted to bring up the budget cuts, but the manager broke the ice at the team meeting."

It is important to know the emotional tone that "break the ice" carries. It is almost always:

  • Positive or neutral — It describes a helpful, relieving action.
  • Courageous — The person who breaks the ice is usually being brave, because starting a conversation or raising a topic when everyone else is hesitant takes a little nerve.
  • Social and human — It is deeply about human connection. It implies that once the ice is broken, warmth and genuine communication can happen.

You would never use this idiom to describe something negative. Breaking the ice is always seen as a good thing — the relief that comes after it is what everyone was hoping for.

The noun form of this idiom is "icebreaker," and it refers to the specific thing — the action, question, joke, game, or gesture — that was used to break the ice.

Examples of real-world icebreakers:

  • A teacher asking students, "What's one weird talent you have?" on the first day of class.
  • A manager starting a meeting with a fun trivia question.
  • Someone at a party saying, "Okay, worst meal you've ever eaten — go!"
  • Offering to get someone a drink.
  • Sharing a funny or embarrassing personal story.

Basically, an icebreaker is any small, low-stakes social move designed to ease tension and invite others to open up.

While learning "break the ice," it helps to know a few related expressions that carry similar meaning:

"Warm up to someone" — To gradually become more comfortable and friendly with a person over time.
→ "It took a while, but she really warmed up to her new colleagues."

"Get the ball rolling" — To start something; to make the first move to get a process going. (This is slightly broader than "break the ice" — it can apply to projects and tasks, not just social situations.)
→ "Let's get the ball rolling on this project."

"Put someone at ease" — To make someone feel calm, comfortable, and less anxious.
→ "His friendly smile immediately put her at ease."
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

• Meaning: To say or do something that relieves awkwardness and makes people feel comfortable, especially at the start of a social situation.
  • Origin: From the literal practice of sending ships to break frozen ice so that trade ships could pass through.
  • Tone: Positive, courageous, warm.
  • Noun form: An "icebreaker" is the specific thing used to break the ice.
  • Used in: Social gatherings, workplaces, first meetings, difficult conversations, romantic situations, and group settings.

The next time you walk into an awkward situation and decide to say something friendly, funny, or brave to get the conversation going — you are breaking the ice. And that is always a good thing.
